‘You hear it then, the song that has no sound,’ the apparition whispered, its form shimmering like heat-haze above the worn pianoforte. ‘You hear the sorrow of a silenced string.’ Leo’s heart, which had been beating a frantic tattoo against his ribs, grew steady. He looked not at the shimmering man, but at the yellowed ivory keys.

‘It is the saddest music I have ever known,’ he said quietly. ‘And the most beautiful.’

‘Ah, but it is incomplete,’ the spirit sighed, and the sound was like the rustling of old sheet music. ‘It is a melody without an end, and so I am a soul without rest. I am trapped between the notes, you see. To have no crescendo, and no diminuendo. To be forever in a key of longing, to be an unresolved chord, to be unforgiven. You are a musician. You can give my music its final rest, for Art is your companion, and Art is more eternal than Oblivion is.’

Leo felt a sudden chill, a coolness that had nothing to do with the evening air. He felt as if he were part of some strange and solemn opera. Then the Spirit spoke again, his voice now like the faint hum of a tuning-fork. ‘Have you not seen the inscription, carved into the underside of the lid?’

‘Yes, many times,’ answered the boy, his fingers hovering over the keys; ‘I thought it was just a maker’s flourish. It is written in elegant, swirling script, and some of the words are faded. It has but six lines:

When a hand of gentle grace
Finds the sorrow in this place,
When a selfless artist plays
To conclude another’s days,
Then the phantom tune shall cease
And this house will know its peace.

But I do not understand its meaning.’

‘It means,’ the spirit said, with an echo of infinite regret, ‘that you must play for me the end of my sonata, for my hands are but mist, and feel for me its final, glorious ache, for my heart is but memory. And then, if your gift has always been pure, and your heart true, the Muse of Silence will grant me release. You may hear dissonant whispers from the shadows, and frightful things may try to distract your hands, but they cannot touch you, for against the honesty of a true artist the forces of chaos have no power.’

Leo gave no reply, and the Spirit seemed to shrink in on himself, his light dimming with a desperate flicker. Then, the boy sat down properly on the stool, his back straight and his young face set with determination. ‘I am not afraid,’ he said, ‘and I will play your sonata until the end.’

A soft cry, like a single, perfect flute note, escaped the spirit. He drifted towards Leo and gestured to the keys with a hand that was as transparent as glass. His presence was not cold, but carried the faint warmth of a recently snuffed candle, and a scent of old wood and rosin. Leo did not hesitate, but placed his hands upon the keys and began to play. From the dark corners of the room, little porcelain figures on the mantelpiece seemed to turn their heads. ‘Do not play! young Leo,’ they seemed to murmur, ‘do not play!’ but the Spirit’s light grew brighter, and Leo’s fingers danced over the keys. Hideous gargoyles carved into the legs of a great oak table seemed to scowl and gnash their wooden teeth. ‘Cease your tune! young Leo, cease!’ they growled, but the music swelled more passionately, and Leo did not hear. When he reached the final, tumultuous passage, the Spirit hovered directly over him, and hummed a few notes that Leo had never heard before but understood instantly. He saw the very walls of the room begin to ripple like water, and a profound, resonant silence began to gather in the air. ‘Now, now,’ urged the Spirit, ‘before the moment is lost,’ and, in an instant, Leo played the final, thundering chord, and the Music Room was empty.

CHAPTER IX

NOT five minutes later, the great bell tolled for supper, and, as Leo did not appear, his aunt, Lady Albright, sent a maid to fetch him from the Music Room. The maid returned shortly thereafter, her face pale, and declared that she could not find Master Leo anywhere. As he was often given to wandering the grounds to watch the sunset, Lady Albright was not immediately concerned, but when nine o’clock chimed from the grandfather clock, and Leo had still not returned, she became quite distressed, and sent the gardeners out with lanterns to search the gardens, while she and Lord Albright went through every chamber in the manor. At half-past nine the gardeners came back to report that there was no sign of the boy in the gardens or by the lake. The entire household was now in a state of high alarm, and did not know what to think, when Lord Albright recalled, with a jolt, that he had seen a travelling fair setting up in the meadow beyond their woods. He therefore set off at once for the fairground, where he supposed the boy might have wandered, accompanied by his eldest son, Robert, and the head groom. Young Miss Ainsworth, a neighbour’s daughter who was visiting and was known to be deeply fond of Leo, pleaded to be allowed to join them, but Lord Albright would not hear of it, as he feared the fair folk might be rough.

On his arrival, however, he discovered the fair was mostly packed up and preparing to leave. The fire-eater was dousing his torches and a few painted wagons were already creaking towards the road. Having sent Robert and the groom to question the carnies, he hurried back to the manor and dispatched a rider to the constabulary in the village, with a description of a young boy who might have stowed away with a travelling show. He then had his own horse saddled and, after begging his wife and Miss Ainsworth to take some broth, rode off towards the old King’s Highway with the groom. He had scarcely gone a mile when he heard the frantic drumming of hooves behind him, and, turning, saw his son Robert approaching at a gallop on his hunter, his hair flying in the wind.

‘I’m dreadfully sorry, Father,’ Robert panted, ‘but I cannot rest while Leo is gone. Miss Ainsworth is beside herself with grief! Please, do not be cross with me; you know how he looks up to me. You won’t make me go back, will you? I must not! I will not!’

Lord Albright could not suppress a faint smile at the boy’s earnest chivalry, and was rather moved by his loyalty to his younger cousin, so leaning across from his saddle, he clapped him on the shoulder and said, ‘Well, Robert, if you will not go back, then you must ride with me, but for heaven’s sake try to keep up.’

‘Oh, thank you, Father! I knew you would see reason!’ cried the boy, and they galloped on towards the crossroads. There Lord Albright questioned the watchman if a boy matching Leo’s description had passed by, but he had seen nothing of the sort. The watchman, however, promised to keep a sharp lookout, and, after a moment’s thought, Lord Albright turned his horse towards Blackwood End, a small hamlet that was notorious as a resting place for vagrants and performers, as it had a large, unregulated common. Here they woke the local publican, but could get no useful intelligence from him, and, after riding across the length of the misty common, they turned their horses for home, arriving at the Manor near midnight, exhausted and utterly dispirited.

They found the gardeners waiting at the main gate with lanterns, for the long drive was shrouded in darkness. Not a trace of Leo had been found. The fair folk had been stopped on the road to Brighton, but he was not among them, and they explained their early departure by swearing they had a pressing engagement at the Lewes races and could not afford to be late. Indeed, they seemed most concerned to hear of the boy’s disappearance, as they were indebted to Lord Albright for the use of his meadow, and three of their strongest men had even volunteered to double back and assist in the search. The boathouse had been opened, and the entire estate grounds combed over, but to no avail. It was quite clear that, for this night at least, Leo was truly gone; and it was with the heaviest of hearts that Lord Albright and his son dismounted and walked towards the house, the groom leading the tired horses behind them. In the entrance hall they found a huddle of weeping maids, and collapsed on a chaise longue in the drawing-room was poor Lady Albright, nearly senseless with fright and worry, while Miss Ainsworth knelt beside her, bathing her temples with lavender water. Lord Albright immediately demanded she take a glass of sherry, and had a cold supper brought in for the whole party. It was a miserable meal, for no one said a word, and even Robert was silent and grave, as he was exceedingly fond of his cousin. When they had finished, they all sat in the silent, candlelit room, listening to the ticking of the clock, and waiting for a dawn that they feared would bring no comfort.

He sank into a heavy armchair, burying his face in his hands. Robert, who had never before seen his father so utterly defeated, felt a lump rise in his throat, and he went over and stood beside his mother’s chaise longue, placing a hand awkwardly on her shoulder. Miss Ainsworth looked from one to the other, her own face a mask of pale distress, her hands twisting a damp handkerchief in her lap. The candles on the mantelpiece burned low, their flames casting long, dancing shadows that writhed upon the walls like troubled spirits. Outside, the wind had risen, and it moaned about the gables of the old house like a thing in pain. Every gust that rattled the window-panes, every creak of an ancient floorboard in the corridors above, sent a fresh wave of terror through the little party.

They sat thus for what seemed an eternity, each lost in their own dreadful imaginings. Lord Albright pictured his cousin’s son, so bright and full of life, fallen prey to some terrible accident in the woods, or worse, in the clutches of some villain without a conscience. Lady Albright could think of nothing but Leo’s sweet, laughing face, and the thought that she might never see it again was a physical agony that left her breathless. Even the house itself seemed to be holding its breath, the very portraits of stern-faced ancestors appearing to look down from their frames with an air of grim commiseration. The clock in the hall struck one, its deep, sonorous chime echoing through the silent manor with a dreadful finality.

As the last stroke faded into the oppressive quiet, there came a sudden, jarring noise from the far end of the drawing-room; it was not a knock, nor a footstep, but a loud, grating sound, like stone grinding upon stone, followed by a sharp crack and a heavy thud.

Lord Albright sprang to his feet, his exhaustion forgotten. ‘What in God’s name was that?’ he cried, his hand instinctively going to a heavy iron poker by the hearth. Robert, his own fear eclipsed by a surge of protective instinct, moved to stand before his mother.

The sound had come from the wall beside the great oak bookcase, a section of ancient panelling that had not been touched for a century. As they all stared, their hearts beating a frantic tattoo against their ribs, a section of the wall, cunningly disguised as part of the wainscoting, swung slowly inwards, revealing a yawning black aperture. A gust of cold, damp air, smelling of earth and fallen leaves, swept into the room, making the candle flames dance wildly.

And in the opening, he stood.

It was Leo. He was deathly pale, and his fair hair was tousled and damp, with a single green leaf caught in its golden curls. His clothes were smudged with dirt and what looked like moss, but he was quite unharmed. In his right hand he held, not a toy or a stolen apple, but a single, perfect white flower, a bloom of a kind none of them had ever seen before. Its petals, which were shaped like tiny, delicate crescent moons, seemed to possess a faint, internal luminescence, and it filled the little space around him with a soft, silvery light. He looked dazed, and his blue eyes were wide, as if he had just woken from a profound and terrible dream.

‘Leo!’ shrieked Lady Albright, and the sound was a mixture of utter disbelief and ecstatic joy. Forgetting all her weakness, she flew across the room and caught the boy in her arms, covering his face, his hair, his hands with kisses, and bursting into a flood of relieved tears.

Lord Albright stood frozen for a moment, the poker still clutched in his hand, his mind refusing to process the scene before him. Then, with a great, shuddering sigh, he let the iron fall to the floor with a clang, and strode forwards, his own eyes suspiciously bright.

‘Leo, my boy, my dear boy,’ he stammered, his voice thick with emotion. ‘Where have you been? We have been out of our minds with worry! We have searched everywhere, we thought… we feared the worst.’

Leo looked up from his aunt’s embrace, his gaze slowly coming back into focus. He looked at his uncle, then at Robert, who was staring at him with wide-eyed astonishment.

‘I am sorry,’ he said, his voice small and strange. ‘I did not mean to make you worry. I had to go. The Green Man called to me.’

‘The Green Man?’ repeated Lord Albright, exchanging a bewildered glance with Miss Ainsworth. ‘What are you talking about, child? Have you had a fall? Did someone take you? You must tell us everything.’ He led the boy gently towards the fire, while Lady Albright clung to his other hand, refusing to let him go for even an instant.

They all gathered around him, their faces a mixture of relief, anxiety, and profound curiosity. Leo, now seated in the great armchair his uncle had vacated, looked down at the strange, glowing flower in his hand, and began to speak.

‘I was in the yew maze,’ he began, ‘when I heard it. A voice, like wind in the leaves, calling my name. It led me to the old oak at the edge of the north wood, the one struck by lightning years ago. It has a face carved in the bark, you know, a very old one.’

‘Yes, yes, the old Druid’s Oak,’ said Lord Albright impatiently. ‘Go on, boy.’

‘There were words, too,’ Leo continued, ‘carved below the face. I have seen them before but never understood them. They were covered in moss. But to-night, the moss seemed to glow, and I could read them quite clearly. They said:

When a heart of gold is freely given,
When the weeping stone is riven,
When a loyal child, with courage true,
Pays the ancient forest’s due,
Then shall peace return to the wood,
And all be right and all be good.

But I did not know what they meant.’

‘They meant,’ said a voice so deep and sad it seemed to come from the earth itself, ‘that you had to help me.’ Leo’s eyes were unfocused again, as if he were re-living the moment. ‘The voice came from the tree itself. It told me it was the spirit of the wood, and that its heart was broken because its tree was dying, and men had forgotten it. It was trapped between life and death, and could find no peace. It told me it had been waiting for a child with a loyal heart, a child who could hear its call.’

‘Good heavens,’ muttered Lord Albright, staring at his nephew as if he had taken leave of his senses. Lady Albright, however, merely clutched her son tighter, her eyes full of a wondering tenderness.

‘The spirit said I must give it a “heart of gold” to pay the forest’s due,’ Leo went on, his voice gaining a little strength. ‘I did not have one, but then I remembered my locket, the one Mama gave me, with her picture inside. It is gold, you see. I took it from my neck, and I said that he could have it, if it would help him be at peace. I held it out, and a crack appeared in the trunk of the old oak, and a hand, made of bark and twisted roots, came out and took it from me.’

A collective gasp went through the room.

‘Then the tree opened,’ said Leo, his eyes wide with the memory of it, ‘and the Green Man led me inside. It was not dark, like you would think. The roots were like the arches of a great church, and glowing moss grew everywhere, and there was a sound like a thousand leaves whispering secrets. He told me that my gift had freed him, because it was given from love, and that the forest would now be at peace. He showed me fearful things in the shadows, shapes made of old sorrow and anger, but he held my hand and they could not touch me. And then he gave me this flower. He said it is a Moonpetal, and that it will never fade, a token of a forest’s gratitude. Then he showed me a hidden way, a long, dark tunnel. He told me to walk and not be afraid, and at the end of it was the wall, and it opened for me.’

He finished his extraordinary tale and looked up at the circle of stunned faces. For a long moment, no one spoke. The only sounds were the crackling of the fire and Lady Albright’s quiet weeping.

Lord Albright was the first to find his voice. He was a practical man, a man of the nineteenth century who believed in telegraphs, railway timetables, and common sense. He cleared his throat.

‘Leo, my boy,’ he said, with a forced gentleness. ‘You have had a terrible shock. You must have fallen asleep in the woods and had a very vivid dream, a feverish fancy brought on by the cold. We are simply glad you are safe.’

‘But the flower, Father!’ cried Robert, who had been listening with rapt attention. ‘And the secret passage! You cannot say they are a dream!’ He pointed to the still-open panel, and then to the unearthly bloom in Leo’s hand, which continued to shed its soft, pearly light upon them all.

Lord Albright stared at the flower. He reached out a trembling finger and touched one of its petals; it felt cool and smooth, like polished marble, yet it was most certainly alive. He then walked over to the dark opening in the wall and peered inside, but could see nothing but a few stone steps leading down into impenetrable blackness. He was utterly baffled, his rational mind struggling against the impossible evidence before his very eyes.

‘And my locket is gone,’ said Leo quietly. ‘He took it.’

Lord Albright ran a hand through his hair in profound agitation. He looked at his wife, whose face was shining with a kind of holy wonder, at his son, whose eyes were ablaze with excitement, and at his nephew, who looked tired but serene, the magical flower resting in his small hand. He felt as if the solid ground of his world had suddenly given way to reveal a chasm of myth and mystery.

‘Well,’ he said at last, with the air of a man making a great and difficult concession. ‘Well, we shall not speak of it any more to-night. The boy is home, that is all that matters. To bed, all of you. We can investigate this… this peculiar business in the morning.’

And so, after Lady Albright had insisted on giving Leo a bowl of hot soup and wrapping him in the warmest blankets, the exhausted household finally retired. Lord Albright himself personally inspected the secret panel, discovering that it worked on a hidden pressure plate in the floorboards, a mechanism of which he had been entirely unaware. With a heavy sigh, he pushed it shut, and the drawing-room was once more an ordinary room, save for the single, impossible flower that now stood in a crystal vase on the mantelpiece, its gentle light a silent testament to the night’s incredible events.

The next morning, as soon as the sun was up, Lord Albright, with Robert and Leo in tow, went straight to the Druid’s Oak at the edge of the north wood. The ancient tree stood as it always had, gnarled and majestic, its lightning-scarred trunk a testament to its great age. They found the curious carving of the Green Man’s face, and below it, the faint lines of the inscription, just as Leo had described. And when Lord Albright scraped away the thick moss, he saw with his own eyes that the boy’s golden locket was nowhere to be found. There was, however, a fresh scar in the bark, a small, deep fissure right at the heart of the trunk, which looked for all the world like a closed mouth.

Lord Albright said nothing at all for a very long time. He simply stood there, staring at the tree, his brow furrowed in thought.

‘You see, Father,’ said Robert in a hushed voice. ‘It is all true.’

Lord Albright turned and looked at Leo, who was gazing up at the great tree with an expression of quiet understanding. ‘The Green Man said his tree was dying,’ the little boy said softly. ‘He was sad that when it fell, there would be nothing to take its place.’

A strange look came over Lord Albright’s face. He put his hands on the shoulders of the two boys. ‘Then,’ he said, with a new and solemn gravity in his voice, ‘we shall see to it that something does.’

And so it was arranged. A few days later, a small, formal ceremony took place in the north wood. Lord Albright had procured the finest oak sapling to be found in the county, and he and the head gardener dug a hole in the rich earth a few feet from the old, dying tree. The whole family was present, as were Miss Ainsworth and a few of the older servants, who had heard whispers of the strange affair and looked on with a kind of reverent curiosity.

When all was ready, Lord Albright gave the spade to Leo. The boy, dressed in his Sunday best, solemnly threw the first scoop of earth around the sapling’s roots. Then Robert added a scoop, and then Lord Albright himself. When the tree was securely planted, Leo went back into the house and returned with the Moonpetal. He knelt in the grass, and with great care, he laid the luminous, eternal flower at the base of the new little oak, where its silver light pooled upon the dark soil.

‘A gift for a gift,’ he whispered, more to himself than to anyone else.

As they all stood back to admire their work, a sudden breeze rustled the leaves of the old oak, and it seemed to them that the sound was not one of melancholy, but of a long, contented sigh. From that day on, a profound peace seemed to settle over the manor and its grounds, and though the affair of Leo’s disappearance was never spoken of to outsiders, it became a cherished, secret legend within the family.

Several years passed. The old Druid’s Oak eventually fell in a winter storm, but the new one grew strong and tall, a fine, handsome young tree. The Moonpetal, true to the spirit’s word, never faded, though after a year and a day, Leo found that it had vanished from the foot of the tree, having, as he explained to Robert, ‘gone back into the earth to give it strength.’

One fine summer afternoon, Robert, now a tall young man on the eve of his departure for Sandhurst, found Leo sitting under the shade of that very oak, a book of old legends lying open on his lap.

‘Still thinking about the Green Man, are you?’ Robert asked, a teasing but affectionate smile on his face.

Leo looked up, and his eyes, still as blue as ever, had a faraway look in them. ‘Sometimes,’ he said. ‘Do you know, Robert, I still have dreams of that place inside the tree. I do not think I shall ever forget it.’

‘Nor I,’ said Robert. ‘It was the most tremendous adventure.’

Lord Albright, who was walking on the terrace and saw the two boys under the tree, stopped and watched them for a moment. He still, when pressed, would refer to the incident as ‘a most curious episode, likely a trick of the boy’s imagination,’ but he never failed to tip his hat with a certain private respect whenever he passed the new oak, and he had strictly forbidden any of the woodsmen from ever laying an axe to it. As for Lady Albright, she kept the crystal vase in which the Moonpetal had once stood on her dressing-table, and considered it her most precious treasure, for she knew, with a certainty that defied all logic, that it had once held a miracle. And Leo, though he grew up to be a happy and perfectly normal young man, always retained a certain quiet thoughtfulness, and a deep, abiding love for the woods and wild places, for he knew, as few ever do, that the world is a great deal more mysterious and beautiful than it sometimes appears.

‘It is no use,’ he said, in a voice hoarse with fatigue and despair. ‘We have done all that is humanly possible. We can only wait for morning, though I fear what news the light may bring.’

He sank into a heavy armchair, burying his face in his hands. A terrible silence fell upon the room, broken only by the frantic ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall and the soft, shuddering sobs of Lady Albright. Robert, who had never before seen his father so utterly defeated, felt a lump rise in his throat, and he went over and stood beside his mother’s chaise longue, placing a hand awkwardly on her shoulder. Miss Ainsworth looked from one to the other, her own face a mask of pale distress, her hands twisting a damp handkerchief in her lap. The candles on the mantelpiece burned low, their flames casting long, dancing shadows that writhed upon the walls like troubled spirits. Outside, the wind had risen, and it moaned about the gables of the old house like a thing in pain. Every gust that rattled the window-panes, every creak of an ancient floorboard in the corridors above, sent a fresh wave of terror through the little party.

They sat thus for what seemed an eternity, each lost in their own dreadful imaginings. Lord Albright pictured his cousin’s son, so bright and full of life, fallen prey to some terrible accident in the woods, or worse, in the clutches of some villain without a conscience. Lady Albright could think of nothing but Leo’s sweet, laughing face, and the thought that she might never see it again was a physical agony that left her breathless. Even the house itself seemed to be holding its breath, the very portraits of stern-faced ancestors appearing to look down from their frames with an air of grim commiseration. The clock in the hall struck one, its deep, sonorous chime echoing through the silent manor with a dreadful finality.

As the last stroke faded into the oppressive quiet, there came a sudden, jarring noise from the far end of the drawing-room; it was not a knock, nor a footstep, but a loud, grating sound, like stone grinding upon stone, followed by a sharp crack and a heavy thud.

Lord Albright sprang to his feet, his exhaustion forgotten. ‘What in God’s name was that?’ he cried, his hand instinctively going to a heavy iron poker by the hearth. Robert, his own fear eclipsed by a surge of protective instinct, moved to stand before his mother.

The sound had come from the wall beside the great oak bookcase, a section of ancient panelling that had not been touched for a century. As they all stared, their hearts beating a frantic tattoo against their ribs, a section of the wall, cunningly disguised as part of the wainscoting, swung slowly inwards, revealing a yawning black aperture. A gust of cold, damp air, smelling of earth and fallen leaves, swept into the room, making the candle flames dance wildly.

And in the opening, he stood.

It was Leo. He was deathly pale, and his fair hair was tousled and damp, with a single green leaf caught in its golden curls. His clothes were smudged with dirt and what looked like moss, but he was quite unharmed. In his right hand he held, not a toy or a stolen apple, but a single, perfect white flower, a bloom of a kind none of them had ever seen before. Its petals, which were shaped like tiny, delicate crescent moons, seemed to possess a faint, internal luminescence, and it filled the little space around him with a soft, silvery light. He looked dazed, and his blue eyes were wide, as if he had just woken from a profound and terrible dream.

‘Leo!’ shrieked Lady Albright, and the sound was a mixture of utter disbelief and ecstatic joy. Forgetting all her weakness, she flew across the room and caught the boy in her arms, covering his face, his hair, his hands with kisses, and bursting into a flood of relieved tears.

Lord Albright stood frozen for a moment, the poker still clutched in his hand, his mind refusing to process the scene before him. Then, with a great, shuddering sigh, he let the iron fall to the floor with a clang, and strode forwards, his own eyes suspiciously bright.

‘Leo, my boy, my dear boy,’ he stammered, his voice thick with emotion. ‘Where have you been? We have been out of our minds with worry! We have searched everywhere, we thought… we feared the worst.’

Leo looked up from his aunt’s embrace, his gaze slowly coming back into focus. He looked at his uncle, then at Robert, who was staring at him with wide-eyed astonishment.

‘I am sorry,’ he said, his voice small and strange. ‘I did not mean to make you worry. I had to go. The Green Man called to me.’

‘The Green Man?’ repeated Lord Albright, exchanging a bewildered glance with Miss Ainsworth. ‘What are you talking about, child? Have you had a fall? Did someone take you? You must tell us everything.’ He led the boy gently towards the fire, while Lady Albright clung to his other hand, refusing to let him go for even an instant.

They all gathered around him, their faces a mixture of relief, anxiety, and profound curiosity. Leo, now seated in the great armchair his uncle had vacated, looked down at the strange, glowing flower in his hand, and began to speak.

‘I was in the yew maze,’ he began, ‘when I heard it. A voice, like wind in the leaves, calling my name. It led me to the old oak at the edge of the north wood, the one struck by lightning years ago. It has a face carved in the bark, you know, a very old one.’

‘Yes, yes, the old Druid’s Oak,’ said Lord Albright impatiently. ‘Go on, boy.’

‘There were words, too,’ Leo continued, ‘carved below the face. I have seen them before but never understood them. They were covered in moss. But to-night, the moss seemed to glow, and I could read them quite clearly. They said:

When a heart of gold is freely given,
When the weeping stone is riven,
When a loyal child, with courage true,
Pays the ancient forest’s due,
Then shall peace return to the wood,
And all be right and all be good.

But I did not know what they meant.’

‘They meant,’ said a voice so deep and sad it seemed to come from the earth itself, ‘that you had to help me.’ Leo’s eyes were unfocused again, as if he were re-living the moment. ‘The voice came from the tree itself. It told me it was the spirit of the wood, and that its heart was broken because its tree was dying, and men had forgotten it. It was trapped between life and death, and could find no peace. It told me it had been waiting for a child with a loyal heart, a child who could hear its call.’

‘Good heavens,’ muttered Lord Albright, staring at his nephew as if he had taken leave of his senses. Lady Albright, however, merely clutched her son tighter, her eyes full of a wondering tenderness.

‘The spirit said I must give it a “heart of gold” to pay the forest’s due,’ Leo went on, his voice gaining a little strength. ‘I did not have one, but then I remembered my locket, the one Mama gave me, with her picture inside. It is gold, you see. I took it from my neck, and I said that he could have it, if it would help him be at peace. I held it out, and a crack appeared in the trunk of the old oak, and a hand, made of bark and twisted roots, came out and took it from me.’

A collective gasp went through the room.

‘Then the tree opened,’ said Leo, his eyes wide with the memory of it, ‘and the Green Man led me inside. It was not dark, like you would think. The roots were like the arches of a great church, and glowing moss grew everywhere, and there was a sound like a thousand leaves whispering secrets. He told me that my gift had freed him, because it was given from love, and that the forest would now be at peace. He showed me fearful things in the shadows, shapes made of old sorrow and anger, but he held my hand and they could not touch me. And then he gave me this flower. He said it is a Moonpetal, and that it will never fade, a token of a forest’s gratitude. Then he showed me a hidden way, a long, dark tunnel. He told me to walk and not be afraid, and at the end of it was the wall, and it opened for me.’

He finished his extraordinary tale and looked up at the circle of stunned faces. For a long moment, no one spoke. The only sounds were the crackling of the fire and Lady Albright’s quiet weeping.

Lord Albright was the first to find his voice. He was a practical man, a man of the nineteenth century who believed in telegraphs, railway timetables, and common sense. He cleared his throat.

‘Leo, my boy,’ he said, with a forced gentleness. ‘You have had a terrible shock. You must have fallen asleep in the woods and had a very vivid dream, a feverish fancy brought on by the cold. We are simply glad you are safe.’

‘But the flower, Father!’ cried Robert, who had been listening with rapt attention. ‘And the secret passage! You cannot say they are a dream!’ He pointed to the still-open panel, and then to the unearthly bloom in Leo’s hand, which continued to shed its soft, pearly light upon them all.

Lord Albright stared at the flower. He reached out a trembling finger and touched one of its petals; it felt cool and smooth, like polished marble, yet it was most certainly alive. He then walked over to the dark opening in the wall and peered inside, but could see nothing but a few stone steps leading down into impenetrable blackness. He was utterly baffled, his rational mind struggling against the impossible evidence before his very eyes.

‘And my locket is gone,’ said Leo quietly. ‘He took it.’

Lord Albright ran a hand through his hair in profound agitation. He looked at his wife, whose face was shining with a kind of holy wonder, at his son, whose eyes were ablaze with excitement, and at his nephew, who looked tired but serene, the magical flower resting in his small hand. He felt as if the solid ground of his world had suddenly given way to reveal a chasm of myth and mystery.

‘Well,’ he said at last, with the air of a man making a great and difficult concession. ‘Well, we shall not speak of it any more to-night. The boy is home, that is all that matters. To bed, all of you. We can investigate this… this peculiar business in the morning.’

And so, after Lady Albright had insisted on giving Leo a bowl of hot soup and wrapping him in the warmest blankets, the exhausted household finally retired. Lord Albright himself personally inspected the secret panel, discovering that it worked on a hidden pressure plate in the floorboards, a mechanism of which he had been entirely unaware. With a heavy sigh, he pushed it shut, and the drawing-room was once more an ordinary room, save for the single, impossible flower that now stood in a crystal vase on the mantelpiece, its gentle light a silent testament to the night’s incredible events.

The next morning, as soon as the sun was up, Lord Albright, with Robert and Leo in tow, went straight to the Druid’s Oak at the edge of the north wood. The ancient tree stood as it always had, gnarled and majestic, its lightning-scarred trunk a testament to its great age. They found the curious carving of the Green Man’s face, and below it, the faint lines of the inscription, just as Leo had described. And when Lord Albright scraped away the thick moss, he saw with his own eyes that the boy’s golden locket was nowhere to be found. There was, however, a fresh scar in the bark, a small, deep fissure right at the heart of the trunk, which looked for all the world like a closed mouth.

Lord Albright said nothing at all for a very long time. He simply stood there, staring at the tree, his brow furrowed in thought.

‘You see, Father,’ said Robert in a hushed voice. ‘It is all true.’

Lord Albright turned and looked at Leo, who was gazing up at the great tree with an expression of quiet understanding. ‘The Green Man said his tree was dying,’ the little boy said softly. ‘He was sad that when it fell, there would be nothing to take its place.’

A strange look came over Lord Albright’s face. He put his hands on the shoulders of the two boys. ‘Then,’ he said, with a new and solemn gravity in his voice, ‘we shall see to it that something does.’

And so it was arranged. A few days later, a small, formal ceremony took place in the north wood. Lord Albright had procured the finest oak sapling to be found in the county, and he and the head gardener dug a hole in the rich earth a few feet from the old, dying tree. The whole family was present, as were Miss Ainsworth and a few of the older servants, who had heard whispers of the strange affair and looked on with a kind of reverent curiosity.

When all was ready, Lord Albright gave the spade to Leo. The boy, dressed in his Sunday best, solemnly threw the first scoop of earth around the sapling’s roots. Then Robert added a scoop, and then Lord Albright himself. When the tree was securely planted, Leo went back into the house and returned with the Moonpetal. He knelt in the grass, and with great care, he laid the luminous, eternal flower at the base of the new little oak, where its silver light pooled upon the dark soil.

‘A gift for a gift,’ he whispered, more to himself than to anyone else.

As they all stood back to admire their work, a sudden breeze rustled the leaves of the old oak, and it seemed to them that the sound was not one of melancholy, but of a long, contented sigh. From that day on, a profound peace seemed to settle over the manor and its grounds, and though the affair of Leo’s disappearance was never spoken of to outsiders, it became a cherished, secret legend within the family.

Several years passed. The old Druid’s Oak eventually fell in a winter storm, but the new one grew strong and tall, a fine, handsome young tree. The Moonpetal, true to the spirit’s word, never faded, though after a year and a day, Leo found that it had vanished from the foot of the tree, having, as he explained to Robert, ‘gone back into the earth to give it strength.’

One fine summer afternoon, Robert, now a tall young man on the eve of his departure for Sandhurst, found Leo sitting under the shade of that very oak, a book of old legends lying open on his lap.

‘Still thinking about the Green Man, are you?’ Robert asked, a teasing but affectionate smile on his face.

Leo looked up, and his eyes, still as blue as ever, had a faraway look in them. ‘Sometimes,’ he said. ‘Do you know, Robert, I still have dreams of that place inside the tree. I do not think I shall ever forget it.’

‘Nor I,’ said Robert. ‘It was the most tremendous adventure.’

Lord Albright, who was walking on the terrace and saw the two boys under the tree, stopped and watched them for a moment. He still, when pressed, would refer to the incident as ‘a most curious episode, likely a trick of the boy’s imagination,’ but he never failed to tip his hat with a certain private respect whenever he passed the new oak, and he had strictly forbidden any of the woodsmen from ever laying an axe to it. As for Lady Albright, she kept the crystal vase in which the Moonpetal had once stood on her dressing-table, and considered it her most precious treasure, for she knew, with a certainty that defied all logic, that it had once held a miracle. And Leo, though he grew up to be a happy and perfectly normal young man, always retained a certain quiet thoughtfulness, and a deep, abiding love for the woods and wild places, for he knew, as few ever do, that the world is a great deal more mysterious and beautiful than it sometimes appears.

‘I have been with the Ghost,’ said Virginia quietly. ‘He is at peace now.’

‘No, Papa, it is true,’ she replied, her voice clear and firm. ‘The prophecy on the window is fulfilled. The poor, poor Ghost. I wept for him, and I prayed for him, and he has been forgiven. The Angel of Death came for him.’

She sat down, for a sudden weariness seemed to overtake her, and as her family gathered around, she told them everything. She spoke of the dark passage behind the wall, and of the horrid, whispering shapes that had sought to turn her back, voices that promised her all the pretty things a child could desire if only she would forsake her mission. She described the little, low-roofed cell at the end of the passage, a secret chamber where a skeleton lay chained to a great iron ring in the wall. It was all that was left of Sir Simon de Canterville, who had been starved to death by his wife’s brothers. Beside the skeleton were a pitcher and a platter, which had been placed there in mockery, but which were, of course, empty.

Virginia recounted how, as she knelt on the cold stone floor, the Ghost stood beside her, a dim, tragic figure, and confessed the story of his life; his vanity, his cruelty, and the terrible murder of his wife, the Lady Eleanore. As he spoke, she wept, for his sins were great and his repentance was very bitter. Her tears fell upon the dusty ground, and as she began to pray for his soul, a soft light began to grow around them. The wicked voices in the darkness screamed and faded away, and the chill in the air was replaced by a strange and gentle warmth.

‘The wall of the cell seemed to melt away,’ Virginia whispered, her eyes growing wide and luminous at the memory, ‘and we were standing in a little garden full of yew-trees. The moon was shining, and I heard a nightingale singing. And then the Angel came. It was all so still and beautiful. The Ghost, Sir Simon, he called himself, knelt down and the Angel smiled, and then it was as if a cloud of silver dust had simply… blown away on the wind. Before he left, he gave me this.’

She placed the silver casket on the table. Mr. Otis, with a dubious expression, opened it. On a bed of faded purple velvet lay a magnificent collection of jewels. There was a rope of pearls worthy of a queen, great fiery rubies, emeralds like drops of liquid light, and sapphires as blue as the summer sea. The whole family cried out in amazement.

‘Good heavens!’ exclaimed Mr. Otis, ‘these are worth a fortune! Virginia, this is a most serious matter. We cannot accept these. They are clearly the Canterville family jewels, and they must be returned at once. Taking them would be larceny.’

‘No, Papa,’ said Virginia, shaking her head. ‘He gave them to me. He said I had given him eternal rest, and that this was a poor reward, but it was all he had to give. He made me promise to keep them.’

‘I knew it! I knew it!’ cried the little Duke, who had been listening with rapt attention. ‘It is a gift from the other world! You cannot return it, Mr. Otis, it would be a terrible insult to the spirit’s memory! Virginia has been a heroine!’

Before Mr. Otis could formulate a suitably republican and common-sense reply to this piece of feudal romanticism, Washington, who had been standing by the library window, gave a loud exclamation.

‘Father, look!’ he cried. ‘The almond-tree!’

Everyone rushed to the window. Outside, in the moonlight, the old, barren almond-tree, which had not shown a leaf for as long as anyone could remember, was covered from top to bottom in the most delicate and beautiful white blossoms. A soft, unearthly perfume drifted in through the open casement.

‘When the barren almond bears,’ murmured Virginia softly. ‘It is the sign. All the house is still now. Peace has come to Canterville.’

It was undeniably true. The oppressive atmosphere that had hung about the ancient house was gone, lifted as if by a miracle. The air was fresh and sweet. Mr. Otis ran his hand through his hair in a state of complete bewilderment. A disappearing daughter, a ghost, a chest of priceless jewels, and a miraculously blossoming tree were more than his modern philosophy could digest.

‘There is only one way to settle this,’ he said at last, his jaw set with determination. ‘Virginia, show us this secret passage.’

Virginia rose and led them to the wainscoting. She looked for a moment, then pressed her finger against a small, carved thistle in the panelling. With the same grinding noise as before, the wall slid open. Mr. Otis took a candelabrum from the mantelpiece and, followed by Washington and the little Duke, peered into the darkness.

‘Be careful,’ he said to his wife, ‘stay here with the children.’

He stepped through the opening. The passage was narrow and lined with damp, cold stone. After a few yards it turned sharply, and they found themselves at the top of a flight of winding stone stairs. They descended cautiously, the candlelight throwing huge, dancing shadows on the walls, until they reached the little cell Virginia had described.

It was exactly as she had said. The grim chamber, no bigger than a closet, was there. The rusted iron ring was still bolted to the wall, and a heap of crumbling bones and dust lay on the floor beneath it. In the corner were the pitiful ancient pitcher and platter. There could be no doubt; Virginia’s incredible story was true from beginning to end.

‘Well,’ said Mr. Otis, after a long silence, drawing a deep breath. ‘I guess I owe Sir Simon an apology. It seems I have misjudged him.’

When they returned to the library, it was to find that the blood-stain, which had been the source of so much trouble and the object of so much of Washington’s Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover, had at last and finally vanished.

Three days later, in a quiet corner of the churchyard, the mortal remains of Sir Simon de Canterville were laid to rest. The Otis family were the chief mourners, all dressed in solemn black. Virginia laid a large cross made of white and pink almond-blossoms on the coffin. In the afternoon, Lord Canterville arrived, having been telegraphed by Mr. Otis. He was a handsome, middle-aged man, with a pleasant, weary expression, and he listened to the whole extraordinary tale with courteous gravity.

‘My dear Mr. Otis,’ he said, when the story was finished, ‘my family owes your charming daughter an incalculable debt. She has performed a wonderful service in ridding the house of an ancestor who has been a great trial to us for three hundred years. The ghost was always a point of honour with us, you know, but I confess we were far happier when he was not in residence.’

‘As to the jewels,’ said Mr. Otis, producing the casket, ‘I must, of course, insist on your taking them back. They are heirlooms and belong to your family.’

‘My dear sir, I could not possibly dream of it,’ replied Lord Canterville, smiling. ‘I have quite enough of my own, and frankly, I don’t think I could afford the insurance on those. Besides,’ he added, his expression growing more serious, ‘they are not truly mine to take. Sir Simon gave them to Miss Virginia; they were his personal property at the time of his, ah, unfortunate demise, and she has earned them a thousand times over. To refuse them would be to question the validity of her courage and compassion, and that I will not do. You must allow her to keep them, Mr. Otis, as a memento of her strange and chivalrous adventure.’

Mr. Otis, faced with this impeccable aristocratic logic, found himself unable to argue, though he muttered something about it being against his democratic principles.

‘And now,’ Lord Canterville continued, turning to Virginia with a graceful bow, ‘may I say, Miss Virginia, that you are a credit not only to your country, but to humanity. If you would ever consider giving up your republican citizenship, I am quite sure you would make a most excellent Duchess.’

At this, the little Duke of Cheshire, who had been hovering at Virginia’s side, blushed a brilliant scarlet and looked so ecstatically happy that Mrs. Otis felt obliged to step in and change the subject.

When Lord Canterville had departed, life at Canterville Chase settled into a new and delightful tranquillity. The house was no longer haunted, save by the happy laughter of the twins, who had returned to their usual boisterous selves. The little Duke remained as a guest, and his devotion to Virginia was so constant and so touching that even Mr. Otis, who had previously been opposed to the match on account of their youth, found his objections melting away.

Virginia herself was changed. She had lost something of her girlish light-heartedness, but she had gained a new and beautiful gravity. She was often to be found walking in the gardens, and she never passed the grave of Sir Simon without a gentle thought. She wore a simple gold ring from the casket on her finger, but the rest of the jewels were locked away, for she valued them not for their monetary worth, but for the memory of the sad, tormented spirit who had given them to her.

A few years later, she did indeed become the Duchess of Cheshire. After the wedding, as she and her husband were driving away, they passed by the old churchyard. Virginia asked the coachman to stop, and she went and laid her bridal bouquet on Sir Simon’s grave.

‘You know, Cecil,’ she said to her husband as she returned, ‘I owe him a great deal.’

‘My darling,’ he answered, taking her hand, ‘you have a heart of gold, large enough to forgive anyone anything.’

‘I am not afraid of the dark now,’ she said, looking back at the grey spire of the church. ‘For I know that Death is only the other side of Love.’

And so the Americans continued to live at Canterville Chase, and they were very happy. Mr. Otis became a famous figure in London society, where he was much admired for his stories of the Ghost, which he told with a great deal of dry humour after dinner. Mrs. Otis became a patroness of the arts, and was presented at Court. Washington married a lovely English heiress, and the twins, after a brief but notorious career at Eton, eventually settled down to become surprisingly respectable members of the community. As for Virginia, she never forgot the lesson the Ghost had taught her, and she lived a long and happy life, loved by her husband and her children, and cherished by all who knew her for the sweetness of her nature and the profound and gentle wisdom that shone forever in her lovely eyes.

The little Duke sat in a large armchair, looking small and miserable, his untasted supper growing cold on a tray beside him. He stared at the faded tapestry with unseeing eyes, his romantic heart imagining Virginia in the clutches of a dozen different and equally dreadful fates. Only the twins showed any sign of animation. They had huddled together in a corner, and were whispering earnestly, occasionally glancing towards a large oak chest where they were known to keep a curious collection of pea-shooters, butterfly nets, and other implements of torment. It was clear that they were devising a plan of their own, one which would likely involve a frontal assault on whatever powers, terrestrial or otherwise, had dared to abduct their sister.

‘It is no use,’ said Mr. Otis at last, stopping his perambulations. ‘We have scoured the county. Every rational avenue has been exhausted.’

Slowly, with a groan of disused machinery, a section of the wainscoting slid back, revealing not the black cavern Virginia had seen, but a narrow, dust-choked passage. And in the opening, haloed by the dim light from within, stood Virginia.

She was very pale, and there were dark smudges under her eyes, but she was not weeping. On her face was an expression of profound serenity, a strange and beautiful calm that seemed entirely out of place amidst the frantic anxiety of her family. In her hands she held a small, exquisitely wrought casket of old silver. She took a step into the room, and the panel slid shut behind her with a soft click.

With a cry that was half-sob, half-shriek of joy, she rushed forward and caught her daughter in her arms. ‘Virginia! Oh, my child, my child! Where have you been? We thought you were lost forever!’

The boys were upon her next, shouting her name, while Mr. Otis grasped her shoulder, his face a mixture of immense relief and stern inquiry. ‘Virginia, what is the meaning of this? Explain yourself at once! We have had the whole county in an uproar!’

Virginia was gone, and the house, which had once been a stage for the antics of a spectral comedian, now felt merely vast, and old, and empty. It was the little Duke who broke the spell. He had been staring into the fire, his teacup forgotten in his hand, and now he looked up, his young face etched with a misery that was almost manful. ‘It is my fault,’ he said, his voice husky. ‘I should have been with her. I should never have let her out of my sight.’

‘Now, Cecil, that is no way to talk,’ said Mr. Otis, though his own voice lacked its usual confident timbre. He walked over to the fireplace and stood with his back to it, a familiar American posture that seemed, for the first time, to offer little comfort. ‘There is no blame to be laid at anyone’s door, save for the villains who have taken her. And they will be found, I assure you. I have mobilized the entire constabulary of the county, and I have offered a reward that would tempt a bishop.’

Mrs. Otis, who had been weeping quietly, looked up from her sofa. ‘Hiram,’ she said, her voice trembling, ‘do you think they will be kind to her? She has always been so delicate.’

‘They will not have the chance to be anything else,’ Mr. Otis declared, his jaw set. ‘Washington is out with a search party, the twins are scouring the woods, and every road for twenty miles is being watched. It is a simple matter of logistics. They cannot have got far.’

But as the clock on the mantelpiece, a florid French affair that Sir Simon had particularly loathed, chimed midnight, and then one, and then two, Mr. Otis’s logistical certainties began to feel as hollow as the echoing corridors of the Chase. The twins returned, their clothes torn by brambles and their faces smudged with dirt, having found nothing but a startled fox. Washington came in shortly after, his report equally grim. They had tracked the gypsies’ cart for several miles, only to find them making camp and quite ignorant of the whole affair. The reward had, as Mr. Otis predicted, tempted many, but it had produced no results. Every farmer, tramp, and tinker in the district had been questioned, and not one had seen a golden-haired girl in the company of ruffians, or indeed, on her own. It was as if Virginia had simply vanished from the face of the earth.

At half-past two, a dreadful exhaustion settled over them. Mrs. Otis had cried herself into a fitful sleep, her hand clutching a small lace handkerchief. Mr. Otis paced the library, sending telegrams at intervals to police stations that had long since closed for the night. The Duke sat by the window, watching the moonlit grounds as if his gaze alone could will Virginia to appear, walking up the avenue. It was in this state of weary despair that they were startled by a sudden, tremendous crash from the hall, followed by a peal of triumphant laughter.

The little Duke was on his feet in an instant, and Mr. Otis seized a heavy iron poker from the hearth. They rushed out into the hall to find a scene of peculiar chaos. A suit of seventeenth-century armour that had stood sentinel by the grand staircase for as long as anyone could remember now lay in a tangled heap on the marble floor. Standing over the wreckage were the twins, who were known to the family as ‘The Stars and Stripes,’ holding a long piece of string.

‘We got him!’ cried the first twin.

‘He fell for it completely!’ shouted the second.

Mr. Otis stared at them, his face a thundercloud of parental wrath. ‘What is the meaning of this? Have you both taken leave of your senses? Your sister is missing, and you are playing your idiotic pranks!’

‘It is not a prank, father,’ said the first twin, with an air of great seriousness. ‘It is an experiment. We reasoned that if Virginia was not taken by gypsies, and did not drown in the pond, and did not wander off and get lost, which is not like her, then there is only one logical possibility.’

‘Precisely,’ continued the second. ‘She has been abducted by the Ghost.’

A cold silence followed this pronouncement. Even in their desperate state, the idea seemed preposterous. The Ghost had been a nuisance, a curiosity, a theatrical bore, but never a genuine menace.

‘Do not be absurd,’ said Mr. Otis, lowering the poker. ‘The Ghost would not harm Virginia. He was particularly fond of her. Besides, he is a ghost. He cannot abduct anyone. It is a metaphysical impossibility.’

‘That is what you think,’ said the first twin, pointing a grimy finger at the fallen armour. ‘We believe he has developed new and more sinister powers. We set a tripwire, just as we did when he tried to wear this suit before, and you see the result. He is walking about again.’

The little Duke, who had been listening with wide, horrified eyes, stepped forward. ‘But why would he take her? She was his only friend.’

‘Perhaps,’ said the second twin, with the dark relish of a boy who has read too many penny dreadfuls, ‘he is a fiend after all, and he has dragged her away to his spectral lair!’

It was at this precise moment that the great oak door at the top of the staircase creaked slowly open. All four of them looked up, their hearts in their mouths. Framed in the darkness of the upper landing was a slim, white figure.

‘Virginia!’ cried the Duke, a world of love and relief in his voice.

It was indeed she. Her face was very pale, and her golden hair was slightly dishevelled, but her eyes shone with a strange, serene light. She held in her hand a small, intricately carved casket. She seemed not to notice the fallen armour or the astonished faces below, but glided down the staircase with a quiet grace that silenced them all.

She walked directly to her father and held out the casket. ‘He is gone,’ she said softly, ‘and he is at peace. He asked me to give you these.’

Mr. Otis took the heavy box and, after a moment’s fumbling with the ancient clasp, opened it. Inside, nestled on a bed of faded purple velvet, lay a magnificent collection of jewels. There were ropes of pearls, fiery rubies, emeralds like frozen pools of light, and diamonds that glittered with a cold, clear fire. A gasp went through the little group. The Canterville jewels, lost for centuries, were legendary.

‘Good heavens,’ whispered Mr. Otis, who, as a practical man, was able to estimate their value in an instant. ‘They must be worth a fortune.’

‘They are your dowry, my dear,’ he said, turning to Virginia with a mixture of pride and bewilderment. ‘Though what Sir Simon expects you to do with them, I cannot imagine. It is hardly proper for a young American girl to be seen wearing such things.’

‘Oh, father, they are not for me to wear,’ Virginia said, a faint smile touching her lips. ‘They are his legacy. The price he paid for his sin. He said that I had saved his soul, and that this was a small token of his gratitude.’

Mrs. Otis had been woken by the commotion and had come to the door of the library. On seeing her daughter safe, she gave a little cry and rushed to embrace her. ‘Oh, my darling child! Where have you been? We were out of our minds with worry! We thought you had been carried off by gypsies!’

‘I was with the Ghost, mother,’ Virginia answered gently, stroking her mother’s hair. ‘I was helping him to find the Garden of Death.’

And so, as the first grey light of dawn began to creep through the tall mullioned windows of the hall, Virginia told them her story. She told them of the prophecy, of her promise to the tormented spirit, and of the shadowy portal that had opened in the wall of the Tapestry Chamber. She spoke of a strange, grey world where there was no sound, and of the final, peaceful resting place of Sir Simon de Canterville. She did not speak of the fearful shapes she had seen in the darkness, or the wicked voices that had whispered in her ear, for she did not wish to frighten her mother.

When she had finished, there was another long silence. Mr. Otis looked from his daughter’s earnest face to the glittering jewels in the casket and back again. He cleared his throat. ‘Well,’ he said, in a tone that strove for normality, ‘it is certainly a most remarkable story. Quite remarkable. I must say, Virginia, your conduct has been exemplary. You have shown great courage and compassion. Though I must insist that in future, you do not go wandering off into other dimensions without leaving a note.’

The twins, who had been listening with open mouths, were deeply disappointed. An abduction by a spectral fiend would have been a magnificent thing, but a mission of mercy to help an old ghost go to sleep was a far less thrilling affair.

‘So he’s really gone?’ asked the first twin sadly. ‘No more bloodstains? No more clanking chains?’

‘He is at peace,’ said Virginia. ‘We shall never see him again.’

‘Well, I call that a real shame,’ said the second twin. ‘He was the only interesting person in the house.’

That afternoon, they held a simple funeral. At Virginia’s insistence, they buried the little casket of jewels in the churchyard, in the corner by the old yew-tree where Sir Simon’s bones had long since turned to dust. The vicar was somewhat bemused by the request to perform a service for an empty grave marked with the name of a man who had been dead for three hundred years, but Mr. Otis made a handsome donation to the roof fund, which settled the matter. As the last spadeful of earth was laid upon the spot, Virginia laid a spray of white almond blossoms on the fresh soil. A little ripple of wind passed through the yew-tree, and for a moment, it seemed to carry the faint sound of music.

Life at Canterville Chase returned to a semblance of normality after that, though the house was noticeably quieter. The famous bloodstain, which had been the delight of tourists and the bane of Mrs. Otis, did not reappear. No ghostly laughter echoed in the corridors, and no chains were heard clanking in the night. The twins attempted to recreate some of the Ghost’s effects with phosphorus paint and a large dinner-gong, but their hearts were not in it, and they soon gave up.

The little Duke of Cheshire, who had been a constant visitor, became even more so. He had been so profoundly affected by Virginia’s courage and by the terror of her absence that he loved her more desperately than ever. That autumn, when the leaves were turning gold and red in the great park, he asked Mr. Otis for her hand for the second time.

‘My dear boy,’ said the Minister, who was very fond of the Duke, ‘Virginia is the master of her own fate. She has faced down the powers of Hell; I do not think she will be intimidated by the British aristocracy. You must ask her yourself.’

The Duke did so that very afternoon, in the long avenue of lime-trees. Virginia, who had long been aware of his devotion, accepted at once. Her parents were delighted, as they had a deep-seated American reverence for titles, and Mrs. Otis immediately began to plan a wedding of such splendour that it caused a great stir in the London society papers.

They were married the following spring, and the papers declared that rarely had a more beautiful bride been seen than the young Duchess of Cheshire, with her grave eyes and her crown of golden hair. Among their many wedding gifts was a magnificent diamond tiara from the Queen herself, but Virginia was never seen to wear it. She preferred the simple rope of pearls that had been her one keepsake from the Canterville jewel casket, a treasure she had kept back not for its value, but for its connection to the sad spirit she had helped.

After their honeymoon, they spent much of their time at Canterville Chase, which Virginia had insisted should not be sold. The Duke was happy to agree, as he loved the old house almost as much as she did. It was there that she found her own peace was not quite as complete as she had imagined. In the quiet evenings, as she sat in the library, she would sometimes feel a profound and inexplicable sadness steal over her. It was a gentle melancholy, like the memory of a half-forgotten sorrow, and it seemed to emanate from the very stones of the house. The Duke would notice the shadow pass across her face, and his own would grow anxious.

‘What is it, my love?’ he would ask, taking her hand. ‘Are you thinking of him again?’

And Virginia, looking at the place on the wall where the bloodstain used to be, would nod. ‘I am,’ she would say softly. ‘I cannot help it. I see him sometimes in my dreams, wringing his hands in despair. I wonder if the peace I won for him was truly enough.’

‘Of course it was, my darling,’ the Duke would reply, holding her close. ‘The prophecy was fulfilled. You wept for his sins and prayed for his soul. The house is still. Peace has come to Canterville. You must not torture yourself with such thoughts.’

But the sadness lingered, a faint, ghostly presence in the corners of her happiness. She lost her appetite, and her lovely colour began to fade. The family doctor could find nothing wrong with her and prescribed a trip to the seaside, which was his remedy for all ailments of the spirit. Mrs. Otis sent for a constant supply of Dr. Dobell’s Tincture, a popular American tonic, but it had no effect. Mr. Otis, for his part, suspected the drains, and had them entirely replaced at great expense, but the shadow in Virginia’s eyes remained.

It was during their stay in a large, cheerful house on the Cornish coast that the Duke, in a moment of inspiration, took the Canterville pearls from their case. He had noticed that Virginia seemed happiest when she was touching them. ‘My dearest,’ he said, fastening the clasp around her throat, ‘you once told me that Love is stronger than Death. The Ghost knew it, and you proved it. But you have forgotten that Love is also stronger than Sadness. These are not a reminder of his sin. They are a monument to your compassion. Wear them, and remember not his sorrow, but your own strength.’

Virginia looked at her reflection in the mirror. The pearls shone with a soft, warm lustre against her skin. A faint smile touched her lips. ‘No, Cecil,’ she whispered, reaching out a pale hand to touch the cold surface of a ruby that sat beside the jewel case. ‘They are not the cause of the sadness. They are only a reminder of the price of peace. Sir Simon carried his sins for three hundred years. Is it so strange that I should carry the memory of his sorrow for a few months?’ She then looked at him, her eyes clear and full of a love that washed away all his fears. ‘Do not worry, my darling. The fog will lift. It always does.’

And she was right. The clean, salt-laden winds of the Cornish coast seemed to blow the last of the shadows from her heart. She began to eat again, and the colour returned to her cheeks. They would walk for miles along the cliffs, watching the great Atlantic waves crash against the granite rocks below. It was here, in this wild and elemental place, that Virginia finally told him everything. She spoke of the Garden of Death, of the skeletal trees and the silent, listening earth. She described the terrible, beautiful peace of a world without time, and the gentle sadness of the Angel of Death. Cecil listened in rapt silence, holding her hand tightly in his. He did not understand all of it, for his was a simple, uncomplicated soul, but he understood the courage and the compassion of the girl he loved. He understood that she had given a part of her own light to save a tormented spirit from the dark, and that the quiet sadness she sometimes carried was not a weakness, but the hallmark of her strength.

When they returned to London in the spring, Virginia was with child. The news brought great joy to both their families. Mrs. Otis immediately began knitting a layette of such bewildering complexity that it required several consultations with the old housekeeper at Canterville Chase, while Mr. Otis calculated, with great satisfaction, the probable value of a child who would one day be both a Duke and an American citizen. The little heir was born the following autumn, a healthy boy with his father’s handsome features and, to everyone’s surprise, a shock of bright golden hair. They christened him Simon.

On the day of the christening, as the family gathered in the ancient chapel of Cheshire House, Virginia wore a simple white dress, and at her throat, she wore a single, perfect Canterville pearl. It shone with a soft, steady lustre, a quiet beacon of light against the darkness that had been overcome. As she held her son in her arms, looking from his innocent face to the adoring one of her husband, she knew that the prophecy had been fulfilled in more ways than one. Peace had come not only to Canterville, but to all of them, a peace bought with tears and prayers, and sealed by a love that was, as the ghost had known all along, stronger than Death itself.
